sections.html: Xenotoca doadrioi was formerly known as "Xenotoca eiseni San Marcos" and was only officially described as a distinct species in 2016. It is a viviparous goodeid. The species is highly endangered.
Xenotoca are very lively fish that thrive best in large aquariums.

Care is not difficult. Keep them in water that is as little loaded as possible, with good current, medium hardness and a stable pH, best around 7.5–8. Generous water changes (60–70% of the tank contents) do the animals very well.

Temperature should vary throughout the year. Some kind of "winter break" at water temperatures of 17–20°C is important. The temperature should not permanently rise above 25°C. Keeping them outdoors during the warm months, when there is no risk of the temperature dropping below 17°C, is very good for their health.

They will eat any common ornamental fish food, but green food should make up a good portion. This can be given as special vegetable flake food or as scalded lettuce leaves, dandelion leaves, chickweed or similar.

The fish are viviparous. At birth, the young still have the strange "nutrient cords" (trophotaenia) on their abdomens, which supply nutrients to the embryo in the womb, much like the umbilical cord in mammals.

More than 50% of the originally known populations have already disappeared, and the rest show a steady downward trend. The causes are water pollution by agriculture and strong competition from alien fish (Pseudoxiphophorus bimaculatus and Tilapia), which cope much better with the changed environmental conditions than X. doadrioi. Catching them for aquarium keeping has no effect on wild populations. All specimens in the hobby are also offspring.

This is an exceptionally colourful strain; even the females have some red on the caudal peduncle.
